USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the May 10 List 3 hike at 25% and the Huawei Entity List in place, do not fire the remaining ~$300B consumer-goods tariff now, and use the late-June G20 Osaka window to reopen talks on enforcement, IP, and forced tech transfer. Keep the 90-day Huawei Temporary General License as a controlled off-ramp rather than a concession. The aim is to convert existing leverage into a written, enforceable deal instead of opening a consumer-price and rare-earths front three weeks before a possible Trump-Xi meeting.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential. After months of talks that reported progress on purchases but not on enforcement (Jan 30, Feb 14, Apr 3), Trump judged China was renegotiating and raised List 3 from 10% to 25% on May 10, while directing preparation of tariffs on the remaining ~$300B (May 5). China answered by raising rates on its ~$60B US list (May 13, many effective June 1) and by signaling an unreliable-entity list (May 31). The farm channel is the clearest US injury: soybean exports to China have collapsed (roughly 75–80% off prior levels), futures fell after the May retaliation, and USDA on May 23 authorized up to $16B in aid. Markets are pricing a growth scare—10-year yields fell from 2.85% (Dec 10) to 2.12% (June 5), WTI slid from the mid-$60s in April to $51.57, and VIX jumped to 20.55 on May 13—while industrial production has edged down and the goods trade deficit remains about $74B. That is material drag and political pressure in export agriculture, but not a supply-chain/recession emergency: Michigan sentiment is still 98.2, CPI is tame, and China’s industrial output is still expanding. The Huawei listing (May 16) plus Google/chip cutoffs (May 20) adds a second-order threat—US suppliers lose an ~$11B customer and Beijing has telegraphed rare-earth leverage (Xi’s Jiangxi visit May 20; NDRC Q&A late May)—but the TGL through August 19 shows Washington already chose a pause valve. Action should therefore be negotiate, not further escalate: Kudlow and Trump have already flagged a possible Osaka meeting, Mnuchin has spoken of a Beijing trip, and China says it is open to talks while warning that Huawei sanctions poison the atmosphere. Firing the unused $300B list now would hit US households (the next tranche is more consumer-facing), raise the odds China skips a formal G20 sit-down, and invite rare-earth or unreliable-entity retaliation before any text is locked. Rolling back tariffs or delisting Huawei without enforcement language would reward the May walk-back and throw away the only leverage that brought China to the table.
key_factors: May 5–10 collapse of talks and List 3 hike to 25%, with ~$300B still unfired
China June 1 retaliation on ~$60B plus unreliable-entity-list threat
Huawei Entity List + 90-day TGL; rare-earth signaling after Xi Jiangxi visit
US farm-belt damage (soy crash) offset by $16B USDA package
Bond/oil/VIX growth scare vs still-solid US consumer sentiment
Live but fragile G20 Osaka diplomatic window late June

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the June 1 tariff retaliation and the announced unreliable-entity framework in place, but do not populate that list, embargo rare earths, or open a new tariff tranche before the late-June G20 window. Signal that Xi is prepared to meet Trump in Osaka and that working-level talks can resume if Washington pauses List 4 and treats Huawei licensing as discussable—without offering new purchase or structural-text commitments up front. The aim is a temporary halt to the cascade, not a settlement on U.S. May terms.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. After talks broke down, the United States raised List 3 from 10% to 25% (5–10 May) and published a proposed List 4 covering essentially the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods, with a hearing set for 17 June—so almost the entire export book to the U.S. is either taxed or on a short fuse. The 16 May Entity List designation of Huawei, followed by Google’s Android/GMS cut-off and U.S. chip-supplier pauses (20 May), is firm-level targeting of China’s flagship tech champion and a direct hit on 5G/self-sufficiency goals; a temporary license only runs to mid-August. Real-economy stress is already visible: official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in May, export orders to 46.5 (twelfth month of decline), April industrial output and retail sales slowed sharply, and the yuan slid to a 2019 low near 6.90 with 7.00 as the next psychological line. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export sectors, FX pressure, Huawei), but not +1.0: reserves can still defend the currency, List 4 is not yet in force, and domestic stimulus (tax/fee cuts, special bonds) is already deployed. Action should not match the threat with another escalation. China already answered (13 May / 1 June tariff hike; 31 May unreliable-entity announcement; Xi’s 20 May rare-earth visit as unused leverage). Firing rare earths or filling the unreliable list now would likely lock in List 4, accelerate supplier flight, and worsen FX/outflow risk. Unilateral purchase or IP concessions would also be premature: the May collapse was about text/enforcement, Trump has floated Huawei as a bargaining chip, and a Chinese adviser said G20 “conditions are not right”—so any giveaway would be pocketed without a matching U.S. pause. A near-zero negotiate stance uses the Osaka meeting Trump has already advertised, keeps existing countermeasures as leverage, and avoids both capitulation and a second-round spiral.
key_factors: List 3 now at 25% and proposed List 4 (~$300B, hearing 17 June) would cover essentially all remaining China-origin goods
Huawei Entity List plus Android/chip cutoff converts the tariff fight into a tech-decoupling threat; grace period only to mid-August
May official PMI 49.4 and export orders 46.5, weak April activity, yuan at 2019 lows near 6.90
China has already retaliated (June 1 tariff hike) and announced an unreliable-entity list; rare earths remain unused leverage
Possible Trump-Xi contact at G20 Osaka (28–29 June) is the nearest off-ramp; Beijing is open to talks but says Huawei sanctions poison the atmosphere
Further Chinese escalation risks locking in List 4 and FX/outflow pressure; unilateral concessions would be pocketed after the May text breakdown

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets negotiations going too slowly and China attempting to renegotiate; orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi.
China announces it will establish an "unreliable entity list" targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
Official PMI fell to 49.4 in May from 50.1; export orders pulled back to 46.5 from 49.2, twelfth straight month of decline; analysts linked the drop to the latest U.S. tariff hike.
Yuan fell for six consecutive days after the May setback; analysts saw a possible breach of 7 per dollar, a level China would likely defend with reserves to avoid capital-outflow speculation.
USTR released proposed List 4 covering ~$300B / 3,805 lines—essentially all remaining Chinese imports including phones, TVs, toys, footwear—subject to up to 25% after notice and comment.
USTR hearing on List 4 set for June 17; earliest possible effective date around June 24. Trump said he had not yet decided whether to impose the remaining ~$325B.
Chinese state researcher said G20 conditions were not right; foreign ministry said China is open to resuming talks but Huawei sanctions are not helping create a conducive environment.
Huawei Entity List ban under a grace period until August 19; Trump suggested a bilateral deal could include a better outcome for Huawei; Chinese state media floated rare-earth leverage.
April retail sales grew at the slowest pace in 16 years; industrial production 5.4% vs 8.5% in March; fixed-asset investment also weak.
U.S. 10-year yield fell to 2.12% on 2019-06-05 (about -73 bp over the window), consistent with a growth/trade-war risk-off that also tightens external conditions for China.
